task: This is a synthetic writing exercise. Using these fictional reporting notes, write a newspaper reported feature for general readers. Draw only on the supplied notes; do not invent additional reported events, scenes, or quotations. Write from this reporting snapshot as of January 27, 2025. Include a headline. Target 450 to 650 words. Follow AP style.

facts.text: The Apex Dark Matter Observatory operates 1.9 kilometers below the surface in Ridgeline Mine, a former silver mine converted to scientific use in 2019.
Physicist Dr. Yuki Tanaka, 38, has led the Apex detector team for four years; she has not found a dark matter signal, a result she describes as scientifically productive.

Dr. Tanaka said: "Every day we run without a signal, we rule out more of the parameter space. We're not finding nothing. We're finding that dark matter, if it's there, is not what those models said. That's real knowledge."

The Apex detector contains 3.2 tonnes of liquid xenon at minus 93 degrees Celsius; a dark matter particle collision would produce a flash of ultraviolet light and a small ionization signal detectable by photomultiplier tubes surrounding the xenon.

The mine's 1.9 kilometer rock overburden reduces the cosmic ray flux at the detector by a factor of more than a million, eliminating most of the background noise that would mask a dark matter signal at the surface.
Maintenance technician Brendan O'Brien, 52, has worked underground for 22 years — first in silver mining, now in physics. He services the cryogenic system that keeps the xenon liquid.
O'Brien said: "I don't understand the physics. I understand the system. If the temperature drifts, Dr. Tanaka doesn't get her data. That's my job. Drift is not allowed."
The Apex experiment has been operating for 31 months; it has had four unplanned shutdowns, each lasting less than 18 hours, all attributed to cryogenic system maintenance events.

Dr. Tanaka said the hardest part of the job is explaining to students and funding agencies that absence of signal is a valid result: "We live in a culture that rewards discovery. I'm asking my graduate students to do excellent science and possibly find nothing."

Her two graduate students on the experiment — fictionally named Nadia Holloway and Ben Tran — are both in their fifth year; both said they understand the risk and are committed to the question, not the outcome.
Holloway said: "The question is real. Is dark matter made of the particles our models said? If Apex says no, that is the answer. Science needs the no."
Apex's sensitivity exceeds all previous detectors of its class; the next-generation experiment, planned to be 40 times as sensitive, will begin construction in 2027 if funding is secured.

Dr. Tanaka said the null results to date constrain WIMP models so severely that if the next-generation detector also finds nothing in the remaining viable parameter space, theorists will need to revisit the assumption that dark matter interacts through the weak nuclear force.

O'Brien said the location is strange to explain at family gatherings: "I work in a mine. But I'm not mining anything. I'm keeping cold something that's looking for something nobody has ever seen. People look at me like I'm pulling their leg."
Dr. Tanaka said she finds the underground environment clarifying: "No email down here. No cell signal. Just the detector and the question."
The Apex collaboration includes 18 universities across six countries; the detector's data is shared in real time with partner institutions for independent analysis.
Funding for Apex comes from the Department of Energy and four international partner agencies; the current phase of operations is funded through 2027.

Dr. Tanaka said she would be satisfied if the experiment eliminates the last viable WIMP parameter space, even without a discovery: "Closing a door that physics has been knocking on for forty years is not failure. It's the field saying: look somewhere else."
Holloway said she expects her dissertation to be a careful null result: "I'd rather find something. But I will do the most precise null result possible. That's the job we signed up for."
O'Brien said the physicists and the former miners share one quality: patience with things that don't yield quickly.
